The cost of routing hop by hop

In an IP network, routers exchange information with routing protocols and build their routing table. When a datagram arrives, the router reads the destination IP, looks it up in the table, and makes the switching decision from that.

The table is as large as the network: an Internet router has roughly 900 thousand entries, and it has to compare the destination address against them to see which one fits best.

And that lookup is repeated at every hop the packet takes, that is, at every router it reaches.
The expensive work is not done once: it is done in full at every router along the path.
Finding one matching entry is not enough: you must find the one that fits best the destination address.

MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) is a label-based switching mechanism, standard in WANs. It is not a data link layer technology.

A label is added to the packet that identifies the destination network and hides the IP header: the router decides by looking only at the label. Since it is of fixed length and an exact match is sought, it is much more efficient.

Benefits:

  • VPN and quality of service (QoS).
  • Unicast and multicast IP routing.
  • Reduces the switching work in the network core.
  • Can carry other protocols, not just IP.
With IP you have to look for the best-fitting entry; with MPLS you go straight to the exact match.

Inside a router there are two planes:

  • Control plane: the administrative one. The routing protocols run in it (an application that communicates with the same application on another router) and it holds all the information later used for switching.
  • Data plane (or user plane): where packet switching takes place, based on that information.

With IP, the data plane compares the destination IP against the routing table. With MPLS, it makes the decision with the label: a whole, fixed-length entry.
The control plane builds the tables; the data plane uses them packet by packet.

The MPLS domain is the provider's network. The user is on one side and the other, and has nothing to do with MPLS: it sends a packet to a router and the network delivers it at the other end.

  • LSR (Label Switching Router): routers that implement MPLS. They can switch by labels, not just by IP, and that is much faster than switching IP datagrams.
  • Edge LSR: the edge ones. They speak IP with the user and label the datagrams so that the LSR can receive them. The Edge LSR on the other side removes the label and delivers the packet.
Edge LSRs bear the processing; core LSRs only swap labels.
Outside the domain the packet is an ordinary IP datagram. The label exists only inside the provider's network.
Example: the Edge LSR applies label 43

A datagram with destination IP 20.1.1.1 arrives at the Edge LSR.

The router looks at its routing table, looks up destination network 20, and finds an entry saying that everything addressed to that network gets label 43.

It inserts the label and passes it to the LSR.

This is the only time, inside the domain, that the lookup by IP is done.
IP routing happens once, at the edge: from then on the label decides.

The LSR does not look at the IP. It looks up the label in its table and sees that what comes in with 43 goes out with 31: it swaps one for the other and forwards.

The packet reaches another router, which detects that it is going to leave the MPLS network: it removes the label, looks at its IP routing table, and switches like an ordinary router.

The edge routers bear the processing overhead; the LSRs only swap labels.
The label changes at every stretch: 43 on one, 31 on the next.
The label: 4 bytes between layer 2 and layer 3

The label is a 4-byte identifier that defines a packet's destination and service.

An IP datagram encapsulated in a layer 2 frame enters the edge router. It determines which FEC it belongs to based on the destination IP, and what comes out is the same datagram, encapsulated in the layer 2 format appropriate to the egress interface, but with a label.

The label is located between the layer 2 header and the layer 3 one: for example, between the Ethernet header and the IP header.
Because it sits between layer 2 and layer 3, MPLS is not a data link layer technology.
Label (20 bits): the value looked up in the table. Experimental (3 bits). S (1 bit): last-label indicator, because labels can be nested, for example in a VPN. TTL (8 bits): time to live.

A FEC (Forwarding Equivalence Class) is a group of packets treated the same way and over the same path. Switching in MPLS means assigning each packet to a FEC and determining the next hop of each FEC.

A destination with one type of service is a FEC and gets a label; another type of service to the same destination is another FEC, with another label. This way each packet is processed according to its urgency or service.

The label has local meaning: each LSR maps a label to a FEC and tells its neighbors about that association with LDP, a control plane protocol similar to RIP. This is how the entries appear in the edge routers.
It is the LSR that determines which label corresponds to each network; LDP takes care of announcing it.
On the Edge LSR: one label per FEC

LSRs only read the label: the IP header is hidden. So they only decrement the label's TTL; the network header's TTL is handled by the edge routers.

  • At ingress, the Edge LSR decrements the TTL and copies it from the IP header to the label.
  • Each LSR decrements the label's (if several are nested, only the last one's).
  • At egress, the Edge LSR decrements and copies the label's TTL to the IP header.

Without this mechanism, the whole MPLS network would look like a single big hop.
The TTL is just one: it travels in the label while inside the domain and returns to IP on exit.

• IP routing looks up the best-fitting entry at every hop, in tables of about 900 thousand entries.
  • MPLS switches by fixed-length labels, with exact match.
  • The Edge LSR applies and removes the label; the LSR only swaps it (43 → 31).
  • The label (4 bytes: Label, Exp, S, TTL) goes between layer 2 and layer 3, identifies a FEC, and has local meaning; LDP distributes it.
  • The TTL is copied from IP to the label on entry and back on exit.

With this we close the WAN topics. Everything we covered transports data, but does not protect it. In the next unit, Security, we start with cryptography.
A single lookup by IP at the edge; inside the domain, an exact match on a fixed-length label.
Why is switching by labels more efficient than routing by IP?
Because the label is of fixed length and an exact match is sought
Because routers no longer need tables
Because the packet avoids passing through the core routers
With IP you have to find, among all the entries, the best-fitting one; with MPLS you look up one whole fixed-length entry.
The Edge LSR has "network 20 → label 43" and the next LSR has "43 → 31". With what label does a datagram addressed to 20.1.1.1 leave the LSR?
The Edge inserts 43 and the LSR swaps it for 31; only the last router removes the label and routes by IP.
Where is the MPLS label located?
Inside the IP header, in the options field
After the data, before the FCS
Between the layer 2 header and the layer 3 header
The 4-byte label is inserted between the layer 2 header (for example Ethernet) and the IP header.
A datagram arrives at the ingress Edge LSR with TTL = 5 and crosses one LSR before the egress Edge LSR. With what TTL in the IP header does it leave the domain?
Ingress decrements to 4 and copies it to the label; the LSR lowers the label to 3; egress decrements to 2 and copies it back to IP.
At every hop the entry that best fits the destination IP is looked up (about 900 thousand entries on an Internet router).
Switching by fixed-length labels and exact match. Not layer 2. Benefits: VPN, QoS, less work in the core, protocols other than IP.
Control: routing protocols and LDP. Data: packet switching, by IP or by label.
Edge LSR: speaks IP with the user, applies and removes the label. LSR: only swaps labels.
